name: Operate
tagline: Maintain production systems at scale with automation, configuration management, and disciplined incident response.
summary: You mastered the Operate stage—from Ansible infrastructure automation and Terraform IaC provisioning to on-call incident management, runbook-driven response, and chaos engineering resilience testing.
heroSnippet:
# Ansible Playbook & Chef Recipe · OpenShift Cluster Node Automation
---
- name: "Maintain Live Production Infrastructure & Autoscaling"
  hosts: openshift_worker_nodes
  serial: 25%   # Rolling update: maintain stability during server patch
  become: true
  vars:
    ecosystem_drivers: ["Ansible Automation", "Chef Recipes", "Puppet Agents", "Red Hat OpenShift"]
    openshift_cluster_status: "HEALTHY_SCALING"
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure Puppet & Chef compliance agents are active and enforcing runbooks
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: "{{ item }}"
        state: started
        enabled: true
      loop: ["puppet", "chef-client"]

    - name: Execute Red Hat OpenShift Node Fleet Scaling & Security Patching
      ansible.builtin.shell: |
        oc adm manage-node {{ inventory_hostname }} --schedulable=false
        chef-client --override-runlist 'recipe[enterprise_hardening::cve_patch]'
        oc adm manage-node {{ inventory_hostname }} --schedulable=true
      register: patch_result
      changed_when: "'Upgraded' in patch_result.stdout"

learningPath.title: Provision AWS Infrastructure with Terraform Modules
learningPath.description: Write modular Terraform code to provision a complete AWS VPC, EKS cluster, and RDS PostgreSQL instance with encrypted backups.
learningPath.keyTakeaway: Never click the AWS console to create production resources—every infrastructure change must be version-controlled and reviewed.

learningPath.title: Automate Server Configuration with Ansible Roles
learningPath.description: Write idempotent Ansible playbooks managing nginx configuration, TLS certificate renewal via Certbot, and systemd service lifecycle.
learningPath.keyTakeaway: Idempotency means running the same Ansible playbook 100 times produces identical results—a critical property for safe automation.

learningPath.title: Establish On-Call Rotation & Severity Definitions
learningPath.description: Create PagerDuty escalation policies, define P0-P4 severity levels, and write runbooks for the 5 most common production incidents.
learningPath.keyTakeaway: A runbook written before an incident saves 10x more time than improvising the fix under 3am production pressure.

learningPath.title: Configure HPA and Cluster Autoscaler for Production Traffic
learningPath.description: Set up HPA scaling payment-service from 3 to 50 replicas based on Prometheus RPS metrics, and Cluster Autoscaler adding nodes during peaks.
learningPath.keyTakeaway: Autoscaling should be configured and tested before Black Friday traffic spikes, not during them.

learningPath.description: Execute a staged chaos experiment deleting 50% of payment-service Pods and verifying the remaining replicas absorb traffic within SLO.
learningPath.keyTakeaway: If your system cannot survive a random Pod deletion, you are one network partition away from a production outage.

quiz.question: Why is Terraform "state" critically important, and what problem does remote state locking solve?
options: Terraform state is just a backup file with no critical operational function

Terraform state tracks the mapping between configuration and real infrastructure. Remote state locking (DynamoDB) prevents two engineers from running `terraform apply` simultaneously, which would cause conflicting resource mutations and state corruption
State files automatically deploy your code to production on every `git push`
Terraform state is only relevant when using AWS and is not needed on GCP or Azure
quiz.explanation: Terraform state is the source of truth mapping your HCL configuration to real cloud resource IDs. Without locking, concurrent `terraform apply` runs can corrupt the state file, causing Terraform to create duplicate resources or fail to track existing ones.

quiz.question: What does "idempotency" mean in the context of Ansible playbooks?
options: Ansible encrypts all data transmitted between the control node and managed hosts
Running the same Ansible playbook multiple times always produces the same final system state, regardless of how many times it has been applied previously—never causing duplicate side effects
Ansible automatically reverts all changes after 24 hours to prevent configuration drift
Idempotency means Ansible can only be run from a dedicated Jenkins server
quiz.explanation: Idempotency is the property that applying the same Ansible task twice (or 100 times) is safe. For example, `ansible.builtin.apt: name: nginx state: present` installs nginx if absent, and does nothing if already installed. This makes automation safe to run in retry scenarios.

handsOnLabs.title: LitmusChaos GameDay: Pod Failure Resilience Lab
handsOnLabs.prerequisites: Running Kubernetes cluster with LitmusChaos operator installed.
handsOnLabs.desc: Design and execute a controlled chaos engineering experiment targeting the payment-service Deployment. Kill 50% of running Pods and validate that the system self-heals within SLO thresholds using live Grafana dashboards.
objectives: Deploy LitmusChaos operator and ChaosEngine CRDs into the cluster
Write a `ChaosEngine` experiment targeting `payment-service` Pods with 50% kill rate
Monitor self-healing duration and error rate spike on Grafana during the experiment
Verify the system returns to full capacity within the 60-second SLO threshold
handsOnLabs.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: litmuschaos.io/v1alpha1
kind: ChaosEngine
metadata:
  name: payment-pod-failure-gameday
  namespace: payment-prod
spec:
  appinfo:
    appns: payment-prod
    applabel: "app=payment-service"
    appkind: deployment
  chaosServiceAccount: litmus-admin
  experiments:
    - name: pod-delete
      spec:
        components:
          env:
            - name: TOTAL_CHAOS_DURATION
              value: "60"  # Run chaos for 60 seconds
            - name: CHAOS_INTERVAL
              value: "10"  # Delete a pod every 10 seconds
            - name: FORCE
              value: "false" # Graceful termination
            - name: PODS_AFFECTED_PERC
              value: "50"  # Kill 50% of payment-service pods
